To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

teenage childbearing has an adverse impact on high school completion, that individual heterogeneity is an important determinant of high school completion among teenage mothers and that the effects of teenage childbearing on high school completion are greater among whites and Hispanics than they are among blacks.

teenage mothers have a lower likelihood of completing high school, compared with women who have not had a teenage birth, and that individual heterogeneity and family background characteristics are important factors affecting the likelihood of high-school completion.

the negative effects of teenage childbearing on school completion are not entirely attributable to the birth itself, that individual heterogeneity accounts substantially for the negative effects of the birth on school completion, and that the effect of the birth on high school completion is not the same across all groups of teenagers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of individual heterogeneity on the likelihood of high-school completion among young women who have had a teenage birth.
how individual heterogeneity and family background variables affect the association between teenage childbearing and high-school completion.
the effects of teenage childbearing, family background, and individual heterogeneity on high school completion.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
teenage childbearing is not the sole cause of the low educational attainment among teenage mothers, but it is an important contributing factor.
teenage childbearing is a strong deterrent to completing school, but that the effect is reduced by the presence of other factors.
teenage childbearing is not an independent cause of high school noncompletion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

individual heterogeneity and family background characteristics account for about two-thirds of the differences in the probability of high school completion between women who have and do not have a birth before the age of 17.
teenage childbearing is a strong negative influence on high school completion, but the effects are reduced by individual heterogeneity and family background characteristics.

teenage childbearing has a strong, negative effect on the probability that women will graduate from high school, and that this effect is largely due to the birth itself and to individual heterogeneity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effect of having a teenage birth on high school completion is not simply a function of the birth itself, but also reflects the characteristics of the women who become teenage mothers.

the effect of a teenage birth on the probability of high school completion is substantially reduced when we control for unobserved individual heterogeneity.
